newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels vow not to surrender, call for talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels vow not to surrender, call for talks.

text.p: Marxist guerrillas holding 74 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Peru vowed on Saturday not to surrender and called on President Alberto Fujimori to start negotiations on their demands.
"Nobody in here is giving up," was the defiant message that flew from the rooftop of the residence on the 18th day of the standoff.

Under cover of darkness, rebels of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) crawled across the roof of the diplomatic mansion and unfurled three banners in reply to Fujimori's uncompromising speech two days ago.
"Mr Fujimori, with arrogant declarations and without dialogue, there will never be a solution," one sign, apparently painted on a bedsheet, said.

In a hard-hitting speech on Thursday, Fujimori rejected the rebels' claim to be fighting for Peru's poor and condemned them as "terrorists" bent on violence. He has ruled out their main demand that about 400 jailed MRTA comrades be pardoned.
The increasingly bitter war of words replaced signs of conciliation and dialogue before the new year.
Fujimori has not sent his chief negotiator in the crisis, Education Minister Domingo Palermo, since the first face-to-face talks between the government and the rebels on Dec 28.
Those talks secured the freedom of 20 hostages, but a sporadic dribble of releases has dried up in recent days.

In a sign that more men could be freed soon, Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani returned to the diplomatic compound on Saturday afternoon with Red Cross mediator Michel Minnig. It was the first time that Cipriani, a close friend of Fujimori, had been to the residence since Wednesday when the last seven hostages were released.
In the long periods while Cipriani and Palermo have stayed away from the residence, the Red Cross has acted as the only contact between the rebels and the outside world.
"We are maintaining our offer of being an intermediary of information," Red Cross spokesman Ronald Bigler told Reuters.
But Bigler added that the Red Cross could only be of limited help in reaching agreement over the main sticking points in the standoff.
"Eventually it must come to face-to-face talks," he said.
With the two sides giving no ground, there were fresh concerns over a possible violent solution to the standoff.

In Tokyo, Foreign Ministry spokesman Hiroshi Hashimoto said prospects of winning the release of the hostages were now worse than at any time since the rebels stormed a Dec. 17 cocktail party at the residence.
"The situation is more serious than ever before. Dialogue began before the new year between the MRTA and the Peruvian government but now it has reached an impasse," he said.
Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said the release of 450 captives since the siege began meant the jungle-trained guerrillas now had greater control over remaining captives.
"I am not optimistic about the situation, seeing as the number of hostages has been reduced to a level where it is easy for the terrorists to control them," he told reporters.

The rebels' inside the building underlined their defiant stand by hoisting their red and white flag, emblazoned with a mace and rifle and the image of Tupac Amaru -- an 18th-century Andean Indian who led a bloody uprising against Spanish colonial rule.

The guerrillas have mined and booby trapped the residence against possible attack and warned that any attempt to take the building by force would lead to many deaths. No hostages have been killed or injured in the standoff and freed men have said they were treated well by the rebels.
The MRTA, which claims to have taken over the diplomatic compound on behalf of Peru's poor, also laid out two other banners on the roof of the building:
"Mothers, wives and children of our prisoners are also waiting for their freedom. Peace for all Peruvians."
"Today's Peru -- 13 million Peruvians in extreme poverty. Where is the progress?"
The remaining captives included Fujimori's brother, two ambassadors, top Peruvian government officials and about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
